the_law.cross_check: An independent extrapolation from the degree-61 charged ratio of 61.2 along the same square-root slope gives about 60 bits; these agree to within two bits.
the_law.descent: 2r/|F|^2 probes, and |F| = sqrt(2M/c) for M bytes at c bytes a stored pair, so r*c*t_probe/M -- linear in r, inverse in memory

what_it_does_support: The shape: reach quadratic in memory, precompute linear in r. A tool for many logarithms on one curve and never for one logarithm -- 17 targets to pay for itself at 48 bits, about 1700 at 80.
what_this_is: The cost laws collapsed into one statement and priced from measured constants: the charged reach of this method grows as the square of the memory budget, two bits a quadrupling.
why_the_large_rows_are_not_predictions: The lookup cost is held at 40 ns, which is a DRAM miss. At 75 TiB the pair table is not in DRAM on any machine and a lookup becomes an SSD or network access, ten to a thousand times slower, which multiplies the collection column. The M^2 law is clean but its constant holds only while the table answers at memory speed, and the law itself pushes the table out of that memory.
The decomposition rates |F|^3/(3!r) and |F|^2/(2r) treat pair and triple sums as uniform over the group. Well supported at the sizes measured here; not proved at any size.
Constants measured at a 48-bit subgroup are extrapolated to 80, a factor of 10^10 in r.
Collection parallelises and the years quoted are core-years, but the pair table is a shared structure every worker must reach, and sharding it is engineering this note has not done.
